claims.text: Expected (mean) conditional government revenue loss for the Pacific islands group in the event year, in constant 2025 USD. This is a signed mean: simulations with revenue gains relative to the neutral counterfactual reduce the average, so gains are retained in the estimate.

Expected shortfall at the ninety-five percent level for the Pacific islands group in the event year, in constant 2025 USD. This is a positive-part tail measure: it averages only the severest loss outcomes, ignoring gains and moderate scenarios.
Probability that the Pacific islands group records a revenue loss (positive shortfall) in the event year.
Assessment as-of date for the authorized ENSO event risk assessment.
Forecast issue vintage of the ENSO outlook underlying the assessment.

The expected loss and the expected shortfall answer different questions for the Pacific islands in the event year. The expected loss is the signed average of the difference between revenue under a neutral ENSO counterfactual and revenue under the forecast event across all simulations; because scenarios in which the event raises revenue partially offset loss scenarios, this signed average is small. The expected shortfall at the ninety-five percent level instead considers only the worst tail of the loss distribution and averages the positive-part losses there, so it excludes gains and mild outcomes entirely. The risk definition states that positive values equal neutral revenue minus event revenue, that gains are retained in signed estimates, and that tail measures apply to the positive shortfall. This definitional difference — full-distribution signed averaging versus averaging of the positive part of the worst tail — rather than any change in the underlying simulations, is why the shortfall exceeds the expected loss by a wide margin. The near coin-flip probability of any loss further shows that the small mean reflects offsetting gains and losses, while the tail measure concentrates on severe loss years.

The gap between the expected shortfall and the expected loss indicates a right-skewed loss distribution for the Pacific islands: most scenarios produce modest outcomes in either direction, but a small share of simulations combine a strong ENSO event with adverse agriculture-to-revenue transmission, producing very large shortfalls. Planners should therefore treat the expected loss as a central scenario estimate and the shortfall as a tail-risk buffer; neither implies certainty of loss, and the shortfall is not a guaranteed outcome. Convergence diagnostics passing does not by itself establish predictive skill; validation was conditional on realized inputs.

limitations: The Pacific islands aggregate is a model-provided group figure; country-level quantiles were not summed or recomputed.
The expected loss is a signed mean that retains revenue gains; it is not a tail measure and should not be compared directly with the positive-part expected shortfall.
The model is not causally identified and measures conditional association between ENSO conditions and revenue, not causal attribution.
Scope is agriculture, forestry and fishing value added with conditional government revenue transmission; this is not a total-economy loss and not a sovereign default probability.
Price and exchange-rate responses are not modeled; results are in constant 2025 USD at a fixed 2025 exchange rate.
Historical input provenance is incomplete for this assessment; it is intended for inspection only and is not recomputable.
Validation exercises are conditional on realized inputs and final-vintage data; convergence diagnostics alone do not demonstrate predictive skill.
The ENSO extension used is not an official NOAA joint forecast; official forecast marginals are dated and refreshed monthly.
